title: Roman Catholic Archbishop of Washington v. John Doe, Board of Education of Harford County v. Doe, The Key School, Inc., et al. v. Valerie Bunker
description: Whether the retroactive elimination of time restrictions applicable to child sexual assault claims, as contained in the Child Victims Act of 2023, is constitutional as applied to the defendants, specifically regarding the abrogation of vested rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the 2017 Act's Subsection (d) established a statute of limitations, not a statute of repose, and therefore its running did not create vested rights that could be unconstitutionally abrogated by the 2023 Act.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the 2017 Act's Subsection (d) established a statute of repose, which created vested rights to be free from liability upon its expiration, and thus the 2023 Act's retroactive elimination of it was unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court held that the Child Victims Act of 2023 is constitutional, affirming that the 2017 Act's time restriction was an ordinary statute of limitations, not a statute of repose, and therefore did not create vested rights that were unconstitutionally abrogated.

title: Syed v. Lee
description: Whether the circuit court violated Mr. Lee's rights to notice and to attend the vacatur hearing, and whether the State's nolle prosequi rendered the appeal moot.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the State's nolle prosequi was invalid and did not render the appeal moot, and that the circuit court violated his constitutional and statutory rights to reasonable notice, to appear, and to be heard at the vacatur hearing, including the right to attend in person.
defendant_argument: The defendant Adnan Syed argued that the appeal was moot because the State's nolle prosequi lawfully ended the case, and that Mr. Lee's victim notification rights were satisfied by electronic attendance, with no statutory right to be heard or present evidence at the vacatur hearing.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order vacating Mr. Syed's convictions and sentence, reinstating the original convictions and sentence, and remanded the case for a new, legally compliant, and transparent hearing where Mr. Lee is given sufficient notice to attend in person.

title: Clark v. State
description: Whether trial counsel's failure to object to a trial court's no-communication order during an overnight recess resulted in the actual denial of assistance of counsel, thereby presuming prejudice under the Sixth Amendment and Maryland Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: Mr. Clark argued that trial counsel's failure to object to the no-communication order constituted an actual denial of the assistance of counsel, and therefore prejudice should be presumed under the Sixth Amendment and binding precedent.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Mr. Clark must show "actual deprivation" of counsel (i.e., he wanted to communicate but was prevented) to presume prejudice, and he failed to do so.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Court's judgment and upheld the circuit court's order for a new trial for Mr. Clark, finding that trial counsel's failure to object to the no-communication order resulted in an actual denial of assistance of counsel, presuming prejudice.

title: In re Petition for Emergency Remedy By Maryland State Board of Elections
description: Whether the circuit court correctly authorized the Maryland State Board of Elections to begin canvassing absentee ballots more than a month before the November 2022 general election under 'emergency circumstances,' and whether the Election Law Article § 8-103(b)(1) is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The State Board argued that emergency circumstances existed due to the anticipated high volume of absentee ballots, which necessitated early canvassing to ensure timely election results and maintain electoral integrity.
defendant_argument: Daniel Cox argued that Election Law Article § 8-103(b)(1) was unconstitutional as it violated the separation of powers by delegating nonjudicial functions to the courts, and that the forecasted problems did not constitute 'emergency circumstances' because they were foreseeable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision, holding that Election Law Article § 8-103(b)(1) is constitutional and that the anticipated volume of absentee ballots constituted 'emergency circumstances' justifying early canvassing.

title: In re 2022 Legislative Districting of the State
description: Whether the 2022 Legislative Districting Plan complies with Maryland and federal constitutional requirements regarding compactness, contiguity, due regard for natural and political subdivision boundaries, and the use of single-member and multi-member delegate districts, with plaintiffs arguing it violates these requirements and is a result of partisan gerrymandering, and the defendant arguing it is constitutionally compliant.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the 2022 legislative districting plan violated Article III, § 4 of the Maryland Constitution due to lack of compactness, contiguity, and failure to give due regard to natural and political subdivision boundaries. They also challenged the use of subdistricts and alleged partisan gerrymandering and racial/ethnic discrimination, seeking a new plan.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the adopted plan complied with all State and federal constitutional requirements. They asserted legislative privilege to protect information regarding the map-drawing process and contended that the challengers failed to provide compelling evidence of constitutional violations.
decision_outcome: The Court denied all petitions, concluding that the petitioners failed to present compelling evidence that the adopted plan violated the Maryland or federal Constitutions.

title: Malvo v. State
description: Whether a juvenile offender sentenced to life without parole prior to key Supreme Court decisions on juvenile sentencing is entitled to resentencing due to ambiguity in the original sentencing court's consideration of the offender's incorrigibility under the Eighth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: Lee Boyd Malvo argued that his life-without-parole sentence was illegal because the sentencing court, which imposed the sentence before key Supreme Court decisions, did not determine if his crime was due to transient immaturity or permanent incorrigibility, thus requiring resentencing.
defendant_argument: The State of Maryland argued that resentencing was not required because Maryland's discretionary sentencing system, as clarified by Jones v. Mississippi, was constitutionally sufficient, and the Juvenile Restoration Act (JUVRA) provides a meaningful opportunity for release, curing any constitutional deficiencies.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Circuit Court's judgment and remanded the case for resentencing, ruling that Malvo must be resentenced to ensure compliance with the Eighth Amendment.

title: Spiegel v. Board of Education of Howard County
description: Whether the qualifications for, and selection process of, the student member of the Howard County Board of Education violate the Maryland Constitution's electoral requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The student member's election process violates the Maryland Constitution by allowing minors and unregistered voters to vote and hold office, violating the one-person, one-vote rule, and denying non-student adults the right to vote for the position, as it is an elected office with general governmental power.
defendant_argument: The General Assembly has broad discretion to establish and structure the public education system, including the composition and selection process for local boards of education and the student member position, which is not subject to general constitutional election requirements.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, holding that the provisions concerning the student member position on the Howard County Board of Education do not violate the Maryland Constitution.

title: Murphy v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co.
description: Whether the Chief Judge of the Court of Appeals of Maryland acted within her authority under Maryland law when, in response to the Covid-19 pandemic, she issued Administrative Orders that tolled statutes of limitations related to civil cases.
plaintiff_argument: Murphy Enterprises argued that the Chief Judge's administrative tolling order exceeded the court's constitutional authority, usurped legislative power, and violated the Maryland Declaration of Rights, specifically Article 8 (separation of powers) and Article 9 (prohibition against suspension of laws).
defendant_argument: Liberty Mutual contended that the Chief Judge properly exercised her emergency powers under the Maryland Constitution and rules to issue the administrative tolling order, making the claims timely.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the Chief Judge acted within her authority when issuing the administrative tolling order concerning the timeliness of complaints filed in Maryland courts during the pandemic.

title: Mayor & City Council of Ocean City v. Commissioners of Worcester County
description: Whether Sections 6-305 and 6-306 of the Tax-Property Article, which allow some counties to deny municipal tax setoffs while others must grant them, are unconstitutional under Article XI-E, § 1 of the Maryland Constitution, which requires general laws to apply uniformly to all municipal corporations.
plaintiff_argument: Ocean City argued that the tax setoff statutes relate to municipal affairs and therefore must apply uniformly to all municipalities under Article XI-E, § 1 of the Maryland Constitution.
defendant_argument: Worcester County argued that the tax setoff statutes do not deal with purely local affairs because they significantly impact taxpayers outside the municipality, and thus do not violate the uniformity requirement of Article XI-E, § 1.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Special Appeals, holding that TP §§ 6-305 and 6-306 are constitutional under Article XI-E, § 1 of the Maryland Constitution.

title: Leidig v. State
description: Whether the trial court violated Leidig's right to confrontation under the Sixth Amendment of the United States Constitution and Article 21 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights by admitting DNA and serological evidence through a witness who did not perform the analysis of the crime scene evidence.
plaintiff_argument: Leidig argued that his confrontation rights were violated when Ms. Rollo's forensic report was admitted and her findings conveyed through another witness without Ms. Rollo being available for cross-examination.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Ms. Rollo's report was not testimonial under the Sixth Amendment, Ms. Keener's testimony as a peer reviewer was permissible, and the report was admissible as basis evidence for expert testimony.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the Court of Special Appeals, which had affirmed Leidig's convictions, and remanded the case for a new trial, finding that Leidig's confrontation rights under Article 21 were violated.
